extra_misconceptions.fact: Vigorous rubbing damages frozen tissue cells and drives cold blood toward the core, which can trigger fatal cardiac arrhythmia.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing snow or massaging frostbitten and hypothermic limbs restores circulation faster than passive insulation.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Heatstroke victims often display altered mental status with hot, flushed skin that may be either dry or damp from earlier exertion.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Heavy sweating is always present when a searcher progresses from heat exhaustion into full heatstroke.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Stabilizing the object with a protective paper cup and covering both eyes prevents sympathetic eye movement until medical evacuation.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Removing an impaled wood splinter from a searcher's eyeball in the field prevents further cornea damage.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Thirst lags behind actual fluid deficit, so searchers must drink water and electrolytes on a regular schedule to maintain alertness.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Waiting until thirst sets in before drinking water keeps a ground searcher properly hydrated on the trail.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a hypothermia victim's heart if you warm their cold extremities before their trunk?
Which physical indicator distinguishes life-threatening heatstroke from heat exhaustion during a hot afternoon grid search?
What measurement confirms whether a searcher's hydration intake is keeping pace with sweat loss over a four-hour tasking?
Why is it dangerous to pop a friction blister on a searcher's heel while hiking through muddy backcountry terrain?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Three blasts on a survival whistle carry over a mile with minimal energy expenditure, whereas shouting quickly exhausts the voice.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Shouting for help carries farther across wind and rushing water than blowing a pea-less plastic whistle.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Batteries die quickly in cold weather and canyon walls block cellular signals, making a written trip plan left behind essential.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cell phone signal bars guarantee that a hiker can transmit their exact coordinates without leaving a written trip plan.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Sighting the target through the mirror's center hole aligns the retroreflected light spot accurately onto a distant aircraft or boat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Flashing a signal mirror requires aiming the reflected sunbeam directly using only a lucky guess at the aircraft.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Shorter autumn daylight hours and rapid afternoon temperature drops require earlier turnaround times and extra insulating layers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Summer mountain trails require the same clothing and turnaround times as late autumn hikes along the exact same route.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a lost Scout position a three-fire or ground-to-air signal so a search helicopter pilot can spot it clearly?
Under what condition does thick green pine bough smoke work better than a bright signal fire for daytime aerial detection?
What specific cutoff time and route details on a written trip plan tell home contacts when to notify search authorities?
Why is it dangerous to wander away from your last known trail junction when fog or darkness obscures landmarks?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Magnetic north points to the wandering magnetic pole, requiring searchers to apply the map's declination angle for true bearings.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Magnetic north on a baseplate compass always points directly toward the true geographic North Pole on a USGS map.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Grid coordinates always follow the read-right-then-up rule, reporting the six-digit or four-digit easting before the northing.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Reading a US National Grid coordinate starts by measuring up the vertical axis before reading across the horizontal axis.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Closely packed or touching contour lines represent steep terrain or cliffs, whereas wide spacing indicates gentle, flat ground.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Widely spaced brown contour lines on a topographic map indicate a steep cliff or vertical rock face.

extra_misconceptions.fact: GPS units fail when batteries freeze or heavy tree canopy degrades satellite geometry, so paper maps and compasses remain mandatory.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A handheld GPS receiver removes any need to carry a magnetic compass and printed paper map in the field.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to your compass bearing over a two-mile hike if you forget to adjust for local magnetic declination?
Which map feature distinguishes US National Grid meter coordinates from traditional latitude and longitude degrees?
What measurement confirms the elevation gain and slope steepness between two waypoints on a USGS quadrangle map?
Why is it dangerous to rely solely on an older topographic map's printed roads and trails without checking the revision date?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The Operations Section Chief manages tactical field teams while the Incident Commander oversees overall strategy and safety.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The Incident Commander personally directs every individual field team over the radio during a large multi-agency search.

extra_misconceptions.fact: ICS limits a supervisor's span of control to between three and seven direct reports, with five being the optimal target ratio.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Span of control in the Incident Command System allows one supervisor to manage twenty separate ground teams effectively.

extra_misconceptions.fact: ICS mandates plain-language radio communication so responders from different jurisdictions understand every transmission clearly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Every county sheriff, fire department, and park service uses private secret codes on multi-agency search radio channels.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Planning collects intelligence and writes the Incident Action Plan, while Logistics provides communications, gear, food, and medical aid.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Logistics and Planning sections perform identical duties at the base camp during an extended wilderness search operation.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should an arriving volunteer search team check in first so the Incident Commander maintains accurate accountability?
Which ICS section is responsible for drafting the next operational period's search assignments versus ordering food and radios?
What span-of-control ratio determines when an ICS supervisor must divide a large group of searchers into smaller strike teams?
Why is it dangerous to self-dispatch into a search area without registering through the official Incident Command Post?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tracking and trailing dogs need a scent article at the last known point, whereas air-scenting dogs detect any human scent in the wind.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Air-scenting search dogs require an uncontaminated piece of the missing person's clothing before they can begin searching.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Urban search and rescue teams specialize in structural shoring, concrete breaching, and extricating victims from collapsed buildings.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Urban search and rescue teams focus primarily on tracking footprints through city parks and suburban neighborhoods.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Fast hasty teams deploy first to check high-probability trails and hazards before slow grid teams sweep large open segments.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Slow shoulder-to-shoulder grid lines are always deployed before fast two-person hasty teams at the start of a search.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Swiftwater rescuers require rescue personal flotation devices, water helmets, thermal wetsuits, and quick-release harnesses.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Standard climbing helmets and mountaineering boots are safe gear for entering a moving swiftwater flood rescue.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should an air-scenting K-9 handler work relative to the wind direction to maximize the dog's scent cone detection?
Which environmental hazards separate an urban collapsed-structure rescue from a high-altitude wilderness search mission?
What clue log details must a hasty team record when discovering a footprint or discarded wrapper along a trail corridor?
Why is it dangerous to send untrained ground searchers into a swiftwater river channel without personal flotation and throw bags?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Place Last Seen is where a witness actually saw the subject, while Last Known Point is the farthest verified physical clue found.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Place Last Seen and Last Known Point refer to the exact same map location in every missing person investigation.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Statistical lost person behavior profiles show toddlers wander short distances and hide in thick brush, while hunters travel much farther.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Lost toddlers and lost adult hunters exhibit identical travel distances and shelter-seeking behaviors in the woods.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Search focuses on locating the subject through clue detection and containment, while rescue stabilizes and extricates the patient.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Search operations and rescue operations require the exact same tactical skills, medical equipment, and field pacing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Establishing early containment at roads, trails, and ridges prevents a moving subject from walking out of the active search zone.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaving trail junctions and road crossings unmonitored during active sweeps has no effect on the search area size.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should operations establish containment blocks first after verifying a missing hiker's Last Known Point on a trail?
Which evidentiary standard separates a witness's Place Last Seen from a verified Last Known Point on the search map?
What statistical distance ring from lost person behavior tables guides where teams search for a missing toddler versus a hunter?
Why is it dangerous to step directly onto a fresh boot print at the Last Known Point before preserving and measuring the track?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A complete Incident Action Plan specifies search objectives, team assignments, radio frequencies, weather hazards, and medical evac plans.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An Incident Action Plan is just a hand-drawn map showing where ground teams should walk during the afternoon.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Terrain, vegetation density, weather, and searcher fatigue reduce detection probability, often requiring multiple sweeps of key sectors.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Searching a segment once guarantees a one-hundred-percent probability of detection for any clue or unresponsive person.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every team must check out and complete a formal debriefing so planners verify total personnel accountability and record lessons learned.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Teams can go straight home as soon as the missing subject is found without returning to the command post for debriefing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Hasty teams move rapidly along high-probability routes, decision points, and lookouts to find responsive subjects or fresh clues quickly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hasty search teams should walk in a tight shoulder-to-shoulder grid across every square yard of dense forest.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to clue integrity during a practice exercise if searchers pick up every object without flagging and logging it?
Which elements of an Incident Action Plan define the medical evacuation plan for injured searchers versus subject care?
What GPS track log and probability of detection estimate must a team leader report during the post-mission debriefing?
Why is it dangerous to launch a field hasty team before conducting a gear inspection and radio check at the briefing?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Most wilderness SAR personnel are unpaid volunteers who train at their own expense, while paid roles usually combine law enforcement or EMS.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Most wilderness search and rescue responders in the United States work as full-time paid employees doing only searches.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Federal protection rangers typically need relevant college education, seasonal academy graduation, and Wilderness EMT certification.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Becoming a National Park Service law enforcement and SAR ranger requires only a high school diploma and hiking experience.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Emergency managers coordinate disaster preparedness budgets, multi-agency response plans, hazard mitigation grants, and public alerts.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Emergency Management Directors spend all their work hours dangling from helicopters and rappelling down cliff faces.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Professional rescue certifications require recurring continuing education hours, skills evaluations, and periodic recertification exams.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Initial emergency medical technician and technical rope rescue certificates remain valid for life without further testing.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should an aspiring wilderness paramedic or park ranger gain volunteer field hours while completing college coursework?
Which daily responsibilities separate a municipal Emergency Management Director from a field-deployed rescue technician?
What physical fitness standards and medical certifications must a candidate document to qualify for a federal SAR position?
Why is it dangerous to enter a professional rescue career without maintaining continuous recertification in trauma and rigging?
